questions.stem: The SIX major classes of nutrients required by the human body are:

options.option_text: CARBOHYDRATES, PROTEINS, FATS, VITAMINS, MINERALS + WATER

questions.explanation: SIX MAJOR NUTRIENTS — grouped by function: (1) MACRONUTRIENTS (energy-yielding, needed in grams): (a) CARBOHYDRATES — 4 kcal/g; quick energy; glucose is brain's preferred fuel; 45-65% of daily calories recommended (ICMR). Sources: rice, wheat, millets, potato, fruits. Types: simple (sugars) + complex (starch, fibre). (b) PROTEINS — 4 kcal/g; build + repair tissue; 9 essential amino acids (cannot be synthesised): histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine. Sources: dal, milk, eggs, meat, soy. RDA: 0.8 g/kg body weight (~50-60g/day adult). (c) FATS / LIPIDS — 9 kcal/g (most dense); cell membranes; fat-soluble vitamin absorption (A, D, E, K); essential fatty acids (omega-3, omega-6). Sources: oils, ghee, nuts, fish. 20-35% calories. (2) MICRONUTRIENTS (no energy, needed in mg/µg): (d) VITAMINS — organic co-factors; 13 essential — water-soluble (B, C) + fat-soluble (A, D, E, K). (e) MINERALS — inorganic; 16 essential; macro (Ca, P, Mg, K, Na, Cl, S) + trace (Fe, Zn, I, Se, Cu, Mn, Mo, Cr, F). (3) UNIVERSAL: (f) WATER — not strictly 'nutrient' but essential; ~60% of body; 2-3 L/day via food + drink. FIBRE — indigestible carbohydrate (cellulose etc.); not absorbed but maintains gut health, prevents constipation, lowers cholesterol + glycaemic index. 25-30 g/day. NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF NUTRITION (NIN, Hyderabad, ICMR) publishes RDA + dietary guidelines for Indians (latest 2020, 2024 update).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.explanation: VITAMIN C / ASCORBIC ACID — water-soluble vitamin; NOT synthesised by humans, some primates, guinea pigs, bats, capybaras + a few fish (most mammals can make it). RDA: ~90 mg/day (men), ~75 (women); higher for smokers + pregnant. SOURCES: citrus (lemons, oranges, amla = Indian gooseberry, guava), strawberries, broccoli, tomatoes, capsicum, kiwi, AMLA is richest (~600 mg/100g, 10× oranges). Destroyed by heat + light → raw/fresh preferred. FUNCTIONS: (1) cofactor for COLLAGEN synthesis (prolyl + lysyl hydroxylase) — essential for connective tissue, skin, tendons, blood vessels, bone; (2) ANTIOXIDANT — scavenges free radicals; (3) enhances iron absorption (reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺); (4) important for immune function, neurotransmitter synthesis (dopamine → norepinephrine), carnitine synthesis. DEFICIENCY → SCURVY: (a) bleeding gums, loose teeth, petechiae, old wounds reopen, weak tendons (defective collagen); (b) anaemia, fatigue; (c) if prolonged, death. HISTORIC: killed millions of sailors from 15th-18th c. on long voyages — >2 million sailors est.; British sailors nicknamed 'limeys' for lime rations. JAMES LIND (British Navy, 1747) conducted one of the first CONTROLLED CLINICAL TRIALS at sea → showed lemons/limes cured scurvy; British Navy adopted citrus ration 1795. VITAMIN C isolated 1928 by Albert Szent-Györgyi (Nobel 1937). EXCESS Vitamin C: largely excreted; 'Vitamin C megadoses' (Linus Pauling hypothesis) for common cold — evidence modest. OVERDOSE: kidney stones (oxalate), diarrhea, iron overload in hemochromatosis. bleeding gums, poor wound healing, bruising, loose teeth; historically killed sailors on long voyages.

questions.stem: Match the VITAMIN with its DEFICIENCY DISEASE: (1) VIT A; (2) VIT B1 (thiamine); (3) VIT D; (4) VIT K.

options.option_text: NIGHT BLINDNESS / XEROPHTHALMIA; BERIBERI; RICKETS (kids) / OSTEOMALACIA (adults); BLEEDING DISORDER

questions.explanation: VITAMINS + DEFICIENCY DISEASES (MEMORISE TABLE): (1) VIT A (RETINOL/beta-carotene): NIGHT BLINDNESS → XEROPHTHALMIA → complete blindness. Sources: milk, ghee, egg, liver, carrots (beta-carotene), papaya, pumpkin, GOLDEN RICE (GM). Fat-soluble. (2) VIT B1 (THIAMINE): BERIBERI (wet: heart failure; dry: neuropathy). Sources: whole grains, pulses, nuts. (3) VIT B2 (RIBOFLAVIN): angular cheilitis (cracked lips), glossitis. (4) VIT B3 (NIACIN): PELLAGRA (3D — dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia). Sources: meat, fish, mushrooms, fortified cereals. (5) VIT B5 (pantothenic acid): rare — 'burning feet' syndrome. (6) VIT B6 (pyridoxine): anaemia, dermatitis. (7) VIT B7 (biotin): hair loss, brittle nails. (8) VIT B9 (FOLATE): MEGALOBLASTIC ANAEMIA; fetal NEURAL TUBE DEFECTS (spina bifida) — supplementation in pregnancy crucial. (9) VIT B12 (cobalamin): megaloblastic anaemia + peripheral neuropathy; vegans commonly deficient; intrinsic factor (stomach) needed for absorption. (10) VIT C (ASCORBIC ACID): SCURVY. (11) VIT D (CALCIFEROL): RICKETS (children: bowed legs, pot belly) / OSTEOMALACIA (adults). Sunlight + fortified milk + fatty fish. (12) VIT E (TOCOPHEROL): haemolytic anemia in premies, ataxia. (13) VIT K (phylloquinone): BLEEDING DISORDER — Vit K needed for clotting factors II, VII, IX, X. Newborns get prophylactic Vit K injection. Warfarin (anticoagulant) works by blocking Vit K cycle. FAT-SOLUBLE (A, D, E, K) — stored in liver + fat; overdose possible (toxicity: hypervitaminosis A = teratogenic; D = hypercalcemia). WATER-SOLUBLE (B + C) — excreted; overdose rare except B3 + B6. prolonged clotting.

questions.stem: IODINE DEFICIENCY in the diet causes:
questions.explanation: IODINE — trace element (essential mineral). RDA: 150 µg/day adult; pregnancy 220; lactation 290. ROLE: essential for THYROID HORMONE synthesis (T3 triiodothyronine, T4 thyroxine) — which regulates METABOLISM, growth, brain development. SOURCES: iodised salt (fortified with KIO₃), seafood (fish, seaweed), milk + dairy, eggs. Salt iodisation is the MOST SUCCESSFUL + COST-EFFECTIVE public health intervention globally. DEFICIENCY: (1) GOITRE — enlarged thyroid gland; compensatory TSH surge from pituitary. Common sign: bulge at front of neck; can grow to melon-size in severe cases. Endemic goitre seen in mountain + inland regions historically (Himalaya, Central Asia, Andes, interior Africa — where iodine-poor soils yield iodine-poor food). (2) CRETINISM — if deficiency during pregnancy/infancy: severe developmental delay, deafness, mental retardation, short stature, spastic gait. Still affects millions. ACCORDING TO WHO: Iodine deficiency is the LEADING cause of preventable mental retardation globally. INDIA: (a) UNIVERSAL SALT IODISATION programme; PFA Act notified 1997; iodised salt mandatory since 1983 under IDD (Iodine Deficiency Disorders) programme. (b) NATIONAL IODINE DEFICIENCY DISORDERS CONTROL PROGRAMME (NIDDCP). (c) HOUSEHOLD IODISED SALT consumption >90% today (NFHS-5). (d) FORTIFIED salt packets — Tata, Aashirvaad, Nirma, etc. EXCESS iodine: Jod-Basedow disease (iodine-induced hyperthyroidism in older adults with autonomous nodules). GOITROGENIC foods (excess can cause goitre despite iodine adequacy): cabbage, cauliflower, broccoli, soy, pearl millet (bajra in excess). Requires cooking. mandatory in India since 1983. prevented by IODISED SALT.
questions.subject: Biology

_fixes.was: GOITRE + CRETINISM (in children); prevented by IODISED SALT — mandatory in India since 1983
_fixes.now: GOITRE + CRETINISM (in children); prevented by IODISED SALT

questions.stem: KWASHIORKOR, a severe PROTEIN-energy malnutrition disease in children, is characterised by:

options.option_text: OEDEMA (swollen belly + feet), growth failure, skin lesions, fatty liver

questions.explanation: KWASHIORKOR — severe form of PROTEIN-ENERGY MALNUTRITION (PEM) in children. NAME: Ghanaian word (by CICELY WILLIAMS, paediatrician, 1933) meaning 'the sickness the baby gets when a new baby comes' — referring to weaning when mother breastfeeds younger child + older child gets starchy (protein-poor) food. FEATURES: (1) OEDEMA (swelling) of abdomen, feet, face — low albumin from protein deficit → low colloid osmotic pressure → fluid leaks out of blood vessels (pathognomonic — swelling despite starvation!); (2) GROWTH FAILURE; (3) MUSCLE WASTING; (4) ENLARGED FATTY LIVER (hepatomegaly — because lack of protein for lipoprotein synthesis to export fat); (5) SKIN LESIONS — 'flaky paint' dermatitis; hypopigmentation; (6) discoloured thin sparse HAIR ('flag sign'); (7) APATHY + irritability; (8) ANAEMIA. VS MARASMUS: severe TOTAL energy + protein deficit. Features: severe wasting ('skin and bones'), NO oedema, old-man face, normal appetite. Marasmus > Kwashiorkor for prognosis usually. MARASMIC KWASHIORKOR — combined. SAM (Severe Acute Malnutrition) — clinical classification: WHZ <-3 OR MUAC <11.5 cm OR bilateral oedema. INDIA BURDEN: NFHS-5 (2019-21) — 35.5% under-5 STUNTED (low height-for-age), 19.3% WASTED (low weight-for-height), 32.1% UNDERWEIGHT (low weight-for-age). Worst states: Bihar, Jharkhand, UP, MP, Gujarat. TREATMENT: F-75 + F-100 therapeutic foods (WHO formulations), RUTF (Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food — Plumpy'Nut). SCHEMES: Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS, 1975), POSHAN Abhiyaan (National Nutrition Mission, 2018), Mid-Day Meal (1995, now PM POSHAN 2021), Anganwadi services, ICMR-NIN. seen when child has ADEQUATE CALORIES but severe PROTEIN deficiency, often after weaning.

questions.stem: The SUGAR present in MILK is:
questions.explanation: LACTOSE — 'MILK SUGAR', DISACCHARIDE = GLUCOSE + GALACTOSE linked by β(1→4) glycosidic bond. Only sugar found in MAMMALIAN MILK (cow, buffalo, goat, human, etc.); ~2-8% of milk by mass (human milk ~7%; cow milk ~4.5%). DIGESTION: broken down by LACTASE (β-galactosidase) enzyme in the brush border of small intestine enterocytes: Lactose + H₂O → Glucose + Galactose. LACTOSE INTOLERANCE: (a) lactase activity peaks at weaning; in most of the world, it DECLINES after early childhood (lactase non-persistence) → lactose reaches colon undigested → gut bacteria ferment it → gas, bloating, diarrhea. (b) Lactase PERSISTENCE into adulthood is a RECENT genetic adaptation (~5000-10,000 yr) found primarily in people of northern European + some African (Maasai, Fulani) + Middle Eastern descent — linked to cattle-domestication cultures. (c) ~65% of the world's adults are lactose-intolerant; INDIA ~50% intolerant (north less, south more). (d) Treatment: lactase pills (LactAid), lactose-free milk, cheese (fermentation breaks down lactose), yoghurt/curd (Lactobacillus ferments lactose — better tolerated), milk alternatives (soy, almond, oat). OTHER COMMON SUGARS: (1) GLUCOSE (blood sugar, dextrose) — monosaccharide, universal energy source. (2) FRUCTOSE — fruit sugar; sweetest; HFCS in sodas; absorbed differently. (3) SUCROSE — table sugar; G+F disaccharide; from sugarcane/beet. (4) MALTOSE — G+G; malt sugar; from starch digestion. STARCH = glucose polymer; GLYCOGEN = animal glucose storage; CELLULOSE = plant structural polymer, indigestible. a disaccharide of GLUCOSE + GALACTOSE; broken down by enzyme LACTASE.

questions.stem: OMEGA-3 fatty acids, essential for heart + brain health, are found in HIGH concentrations in:

options.option_text: FATTY FISH (salmon, sardine, mackerel), WALNUTS, FLAXSEEDS, CHIA SEEDS

questions.explanation: OMEGA-3 FATTY ACIDS — polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) with first C=C double bond at the THIRD carbon from the methyl (omega) end. Three main types: (1) ALPHA-LINOLENIC ACID (ALA, 18:3) — plant-based, in FLAXSEED (richest: 58% of oil), CHIA, WALNUT, PERILLA, mustard oil, canola. (2) EICOSAPENTAENOIC ACID (EPA, 20:5) — marine; fatty fish + algae. (3) DOCOSAHEXAENOIC ACID (DHA, 22:6) — marine; essential for brain + retina; >30% of retinal + brain phospholipids. Human can partially convert ALA → EPA → DHA but inefficiently (~5-10%). SOURCES: (a) fatty fish (most bio-efficient): SALMON, SARDINES, MACKEREL, TUNA, HERRING, ANCHOVIES; (b) PLANT-based ALA: flaxseeds, chia, walnuts, hemp, soybean; (c) ALGAL DHA supplements (vegan-friendly, direct source). BENEFITS: lower triglycerides, reduce heart attack + stroke risk, anti-inflammatory, vital for infant brain development, possible mood-disorder benefit. RDA: ~250-500 mg EPA+DHA daily (varies by guideline). ESSENTIAL FATTY ACIDS — omega-3 (ALA) + omega-6 (linoleic acid) — body CANNOT synthesise them, must get from diet. OMEGA-6 sources: sunflower, corn, soy oils — modern diets have EXCESS omega-6 + too little omega-3 (ratio 15-20:1 instead of ideal 2-5:1) → pro-inflammatory. Mediterranean + Japanese diets are high in omega-3. AYURVEDA emphasis on GHEE, flaxseed + mustard oil. TRANS FATS (vanaspati, dalda) — WORST fat, raise LDL + lower HDL, strongly linked to heart disease; FSSAI banned industrial trans fats >2% by weight in India (2021). SATURATED FATS (butter, ghee, coconut, palm) — modest intake OK; excess raises LDL. EPA + DHA + ALA types.

questions.stem: ANAEMIA due to IRON DEFICIENCY is the world's most common nutritional deficiency. Iron's main role is in:
questions.explanation: IRON (Fe) — essential trace mineral. Human body: ~3-4 g total iron; 65% in haemoglobin, 10% in myoglobin, 20% in ferritin storage (liver, spleen, marrow), 5% in enzymes. RDA: Men ~17 mg/day, Women 21 mg/day (menstruation losses), Pregnancy 35 mg (ICMR 2020 Indian RDAs). SOURCES: (1) HEME IRON (animal, 15-35% absorbed) — red meat, liver, egg yolk, fish, poultry. (2) NON-HEME IRON (plant, 2-20% absorbed) — dark leafy greens (spinach, methi), jaggery, dates, dal, chana, rajma, beetroot, pomegranate, kidney beans, tofu, fortified cereals. VIT C enhances non-heme absorption (reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺) — take amla/lemon juice with pulses. TANNINS (tea, coffee) + phytates (bran) + calcium INHIBIT absorption — avoid chai immediately after meals. DEFICIENCY: IRON-DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA (IDA) — world's most common nutritional disorder, affects ~2 billion globally, ~50% Indian women (NFHS-5: 57% of women 15-49 anaemic; 67% of children 6-59 months). SYMPTOMS: fatigue, pale skin + conjunctiva, breathlessness, palpitations, brittle nails (koilonychia, spoon-shaped), restless legs, pica (craving for ice/dirt), impaired cognitive development in kids. DIAGNOSIS: low Hb (<12 g/dL women, <13 men), low MCV (microcytic), low serum ferritin (<30 ng/mL), high TIBC. TREATMENT: oral iron (ferrous sulphate/fumarate, 60-200 mg elemental/day for 3-6 months); parenteral iron for severe cases + pregnancy. INDIA PROGRAMMES: (1) ANAEMIA MUKT BHARAT (AMB, 2018) — targeting 6 groups (children, adolescents, pregnant, lactating, WRA, men); 6×6×6 strategy; (2) Weekly Iron + Folic Acid Supplementation (WIFS); (3) Double-fortified salt (iron + iodine); (4) rice fortification. Other minerals: CALCIUM (bones), ZINC (immunity), SELENIUM (antioxidant), MAGNESIUM (muscle), POTASSIUM (electrolyte). carrying oxygen in RBCs; also in myoglobin + many enzymes (cytochromes).

questions.stem: The BMI (Body Mass Index) formula is:
questions.explanation: BMI (BODY MASS INDEX) = weight (kg) / [height (m)]². Dimensionless-ish ratio; developed by Adolphe Quetelet (1830s Belgian statistician), originally 'Quetelet index'; renamed BMI by Ancel Keys 1972 for study of obesity. WHO CATEGORIES (global): Underweight <18.5; NORMAL 18.5-24.9; Overweight 25-29.9; Obesity Class I 30-34.9; II 35-39.9; III (morbid) ≥ 40. INDIAN-SPECIFIC (ICMR/WHO-Asian) criteria — LOWER thresholds because Asians have higher body fat % + cardiovascular risk at lower BMI: Underweight <18; NORMAL 18-22.9; Overweight 23-24.9; Obese ≥ 25. EXAMPLE: adult 70 kg + 1.70m = 70 / 1.70² = 70/2.89 = 24.22 → normal (WHO) / overweight (Indian). LIMITATIONS: (a) doesn't distinguish muscle vs fat — athletes + bodybuilders often BMI 'overweight' but low fat %; (b) no account of fat distribution — abdominal fat is most dangerous; (c) doesn't apply to children (use BMI-for-age percentiles), pregnant women, the elderly (muscle loss inflates BMI relative to fat). ALTERNATIVE measures: (1) WAIST CIRCUMFERENCE — men >90 cm (Asian) / >94 (WHO); women >80 cm (Asian) / >80 (WHO) = high risk. (2) WAIST-HIP RATIO (WHR) >0.9 men / >0.85 women = abdominal obesity. (3) BODY FAT PERCENTAGE (DEXA, skinfold, bioimpedance); normal 18-24% men / 25-31% women. INDIAN BMI STATS: NFHS-5 (2019-21) — women ≥18 with BMI <18.5 is 18.7% (undernutrition); BMI ≥25 is 24% (overweight/obese). DOUBLE BURDEN of malnutrition coexists.

questions.stem: The GLYCAEMIC INDEX (GI) measures how quickly a food RAISES BLOOD SUGAR. Low-GI foods are PREFERRED in diabetes because:
questions.explanation: GLYCAEMIC INDEX (GI) — ranks carbohydrate-containing foods 0-100 based on how much they raise BLOOD GLUCOSE over 2 hours, compared to pure GLUCOSE (=100). Developed by Dr. David Jenkins (Toronto, 1981). CATEGORIES: LOW GI <55; MEDIUM 56-69; HIGH ≥70. LOW GI examples: most VEGETABLES, beans, lentils, chickpeas, rajma, apple, pear, orange, berries, milk, curd, whole barley (BARLEY GI ~28), oats steel-cut, bran cereals, whole wheat pasta (al dente), sweet potato, basmati rice (GI 50-58). HIGH GI examples: WHITE BREAD (GI ~75), cornflakes (~80), white rice (~73), potato mashed/baked (~85), watermelon (~76), sugar/glucose (~100), jaggery, MAIDA-based products, some breakfast cereals. MEDIUM GI: rice noodles, whole wheat atta chapati (~60-65), banana (~55), pineapple, honey. LOW-GI benefits: (a) BETTER diabetic control — slower glucose release → lower + steadier insulin demand; (b) fullness longer → weight management; (c) LDL cholesterol improvement. DIABETES INDIA: 10% of adults (>100 million, 2025) — growing epidemic. GLYCAEMIC LOAD (GL) = GI × carb content of serving ÷ 100 — more accurate because considers serving size. Watermelon GI 76 but GL only ~5 per slice (mostly water, low carb per serving) → not as bad as it looks. MILLETS (INTERNATIONAL YEAR OF MILLETS was 2023, India-led UN declaration) — most millets are LOW GI: Finger millet (ragi) GI 54, pearl millet (bajra) GI 55, foxtail millet 52 — hence rediscovered for diabetes + gluten-free diets. Ayurveda advocates 'chew well', 'eat slowly' (lowers GI further). Also processing matters — well-cooked rice has higher GI than al-dente. smoother blood sugar curve, less insulin spike; linked to better long-term glycaemic control.
